what_its_for: Ivosidenib is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of leukemia (blood cancer) and bile duct cancer (cholangiocarcinoma) in adults whose cancer has a specific gene change called an IDH1 mutation. Your doctor has tested your cancer and confirmed it has this mutation before prescribing this medicine.
how_to_take: Take ivosidenib by mouth (swallow the tablet whole) once a day, at about the same time each day. You can take it with or without food. Do not crush, break, or chew the tablet. If you vomit after taking a dose, do not take another dose that day — just take your next scheduled dose the following day.
dosing: The usual dose is 500 mg (one tablet) taken once daily. Your doctor may lower your dose or have you take a break from the medicine if you experience certain side effects. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and it has been less than 12 hours since your scheduled time, take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it has been more than 12 hours since your scheduled dose time, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time the next day. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store ivosidenib tablets at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original container and keep the container tightly closed. Store away from moisture, heat, and direct light. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking ivosidenib with grapefruit, grapefruit juice, Seville oranges, or starfruit, as these can increase the amount of medicine in your blood and worsen side effects. Tell your doctor and pharmacist about ALL other medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take, especially blood thinners (like warfarin), antifungals (like fluconazole or ketoconazole), antibiotics (like rifampin or clarithromycin), seizure medicines, St. John's Wort, and certain heart medicines. Do not start or stop any medication without talking to your doctor first. Avoid becoming pregnant while taking this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: fast, fluttering, or pounding heartbeat or chest pain (signs of a serious heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation); fever, chills, or difficulty breathing (possible signs of a serious reaction called differentiation syndrome); unusual fatigue, dizziness, or fainting; swelling of the hands, feet, or legs; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, or severe stomach pain; nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that is severe or does not go away; signs of nerve problems such as tingling, numbness, or weakness in your arms or legs; or any new or worsening symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: Ivosidenib may start working within the first few weeks, but it can take several months to see the full benefit. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular blood tests and check-ups. Do not stop taking the medicine even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to. Continuing to take it as prescribed gives it the best chance to work.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do not use ivosidenib if you are pregnant, as it can harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 1 month after the last dose. Men with female partners who can become pregnant should also use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 1 month after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking ivosidenib and for at least 1 month after the last dose. Liver problems: If you have liver problems, your doctor may need to monitor you more closely, as this medicine is processed by the liver. Kidney problems: Dose adjustments are not typically needed for mild to moderate kidney problems, but always inform your doctor about any kidney issues. Older adults (age 65 and over): This medicine has been used safely in older adults, but you may be monitored more closely for side effects.
